stem: Complete the command so the image is built by the registry itself, with no local Docker daemon, and pushed to the `copilot` repository.

blanks.label: Blank 1 — the command that builds in Azure
Blank 2 — what the trailing argument is

explanation: `az acr build` queues the build as an ACR task and runs it on registry-side compute, so an agent with no Docker daemon can still produce and push an image. Like `docker build`, the final positional argument is the build context — the folder sent to the builder.

stem: Complete the command so the AKS cluster can pull from the registry without a stored credential.
code:
az aks update \
  --name copilot-aks \
  --resource-group copilot-rg \
  [1] contosoacr

blanks.label: What the command grants behind the scenes

choices.text: The AcrPull role on the registry, to the cluster's kubelet identity
An imagePullSecret containing the registry admin password
The Contributor role on the registry, to the cluster identity

explanation: `--attach-acr` creates a role assignment rather than a secret: the kubelet identity is granted **AcrPull** on the registry, so nodes authenticate with a managed identity and there is no imagePullSecret to rotate or leak.

objective: Implement solutions with Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Complete the command that allows the `vector` extension on a flexible server, before `CREATE EXTENSION` can succeed in the database.
code:
az postgres flexible-server parameter set \
  --resource-group copilot-rg \
  --server-name copilot-pg \
  --name [1] \
  --value vector

blanks.label: What still has to happen afterwards

choices.text: Run `CREATE EXTENSION vector;` in each database that needs it
Nothing — the extension is enabled in every database automatically
Restart the server before the extension appears

explanation: `azure.extensions` is the server-level allow-list of extensions; it permits the extension without installing it. Each database still needs its own `CREATE EXTENSION vector;`. Getting this order wrong is the usual cause of `extension "vector" is not allow-listed`.

stem: Complete the commands so the container app reads a Key Vault secret using its own identity, with nothing sensitive in configuration.
code:
az containerapp identity assign \
  --name copilot-api --resource-group copilot-rg [1]

az role assignment create \
  --assignee $PRINCIPAL_ID \
  --role "[2]" \
  --scope $VAULT_ID

blanks.label: Blank 2 — the least-privilege role for reading secret values

explanation: A system-assigned identity is created and rotated by the platform, so no credential reaches configuration. **Key Vault Secrets User** grants reading secret values; **Key Vault Reader** only reads the vault's metadata and properties, which is the distinction the exam tests.

objective: Instrument solutions to support monitoring and logging
stem: Complete the KQL so it reports the 95th percentile duration of the embedding dependency, in fifteen-minute buckets.
code:
dependencies
| where timestamp > ago(6h) and name has "embeddings"
| summarize [1](duration, 95) by [2](timestamp, 15m)
| order by timestamp asc
explanation: `percentile(duration, 95)` gives the p95, and `bin(timestamp, 15m)` rounds each row down to a bucket boundary so `summarize` groups by interval. `bin` is the operator behind almost every time-series chart in Application Insights.

objective: Implement solutions with Azure Database for PostgreSQL
stem: Contoso must hold p95 retrieval under 150 ms across four million chunks. Which index choice best fits, given documents arrive continuously?

options.text: HNSW, effective as rows are inserted
IVFFlat built once before ingestion begins
No vector index, relying on a sequential scan
A B-tree index on the embedding column

explanation: Continuous ingestion is what decides it. IVFFlat computes its centroids from the rows present when the index is built, so an index created before the load is arbitrary and needs rebuilding. HNSW builds a graph incrementally and stays useful as rows arrive, which is why it suits a corpus that never stops growing.

whyWrong.B: Building IVFFlat before the data exists is precisely the failure mode — the centroids describe nothing.
whyWrong.C: A sequential scan over four million vectors will not meet a 150 ms budget.
whyWrong.D: A B-tree cannot answer nearest-neighbour queries; it needs a vector operator class.

docs.title: How to optimize performance when using pgvector

hint: The corpus never stops growing. Ask which index needs to see the data before it can decide its structure.

stem: The embedding worker must cost nothing while no documents are waiting. What does that require, given the team will not use Kubernetes?

options.text: A Container App with `minReplicas: 0` and a queue rule
A Container App with `minReplicas: 1`, always ready
An AKS deployment scaled to zero by the cluster autoscaler
An App Service plan with Always On disabled

explanation: Scale to zero needs both halves: `minReplicas: 0` allows it, and a scale rule is what brings it back. A worker with no ingress and no rule would drop to zero and never wake, which is the trap in this requirement.

whyWrong.B: One replica always running is exactly the cost the requirement rules out.
whyWrong.C: AKS is excluded by the constraint, and the team wants no Kubernetes.
whyWrong.D: Disabling Always On lets the app idle but the plan is still billed.

docs.title: Set scaling rules in Azure Container Apps

hint: Two settings are needed, not one. Allowing zero is easy; ask what is responsible for bringing it back up.

stem: No secrets may live in application configuration. Which two changes satisfy that for the API's access to Azure OpenAI and PostgreSQL? Choose two.

options.text: Give the app a managed identity for Azure OpenAI
Use Entra authentication to PostgreSQL
Move the API key into a Container Apps secret and reference it with `secretref:`
Store the connection string in App Configuration rather than an environment variable
Encrypt the key and put the ciphertext in the container image

explanation: The only way to have no secret is to have no secret. A managed identity plus Entra authentication on both dependencies removes the credential entirely rather than relocating it.

whyWrong.C: A Container Apps secret is a better home than plain configuration, but a stored key is still a stored key.
whyWrong.D: App Configuration holds settings; a connection string there is still a credential in configuration.
whyWrong.E: The image now carries both the ciphertext and, somewhere, the means to decrypt it.

docs.title: Managed identities in Azure Container Apps

hint: Read the constraint literally. Two of these relocate a secret; two remove the need for one.

stem: The nightly job is terminated at roughly the same elapsed time on every run. What explains that, and what fixes it while keeping the no-idle-replica requirement?

options.text: The function timeout; restructure as a durable fan-out
Cosmos DB throttling; raise provisioned throughput for the duration of the run
A memory limit; move to a Premium plan with larger instances
The nightly schedule overlapping itself; change the cron expression

explanation: Failing at the same elapsed time every run is the signature of a timeout rather than load. Consumption caps a single execution, so the fix is to stop doing all the work in one execution — a fan-out gives many short activities. Premium would also solve the timeout, but it keeps a warm instance, which this requirement forbids.

whyWrong.B: Throttling is real here but it produces 429s in bursts, not termination at a fixed elapsed time.
whyWrong.C: A memory limit would fail at a data-dependent point, and Premium keeps a replica alive.
whyWrong.D: An overlapping schedule would show up as concurrent runs, not a consistent cut-off.

hint: The clue is *the same elapsed time*, not the same document. Ask what is measured in time rather than in work done.

objective: Implement solutions that use Azure Cosmos DB
stem: Fabrikam wants to keep the existing account and partition key. Which change most directly reduces the 429s concentrated on the largest publisher?

options.text: Bulk execution with retry-after handling
Increase provisioned RU/s on the container until the bursts stop
Switch the container to a synthetic partition key combining publisher and date
Enable the analytical store on the container

explanation: A hot logical partition can only ever use its share of the container's throughput, so the constraint here is structural. With the partition key fixed, the realistic remedies are smoothing the write rate and honouring `retry-after` rather than buying throughput that the hot partition cannot reach.

whyWrong.B: Throughput is divided across physical partitions, so most of the increase lands where there is no pressure.
whyWrong.C: This is the correct long-term fix, but it changes the partition key, which the requirement rules out.
whyWrong.D: The analytical store serves analytics; it does nothing for transactional write throttling.

docs.title: Diagnose and troubleshoot request rate too large

hint: One option is genuinely the best engineering answer but breaks a stated constraint. Read the constraints before the options.

objective: Instrument solutions to support monitoring and logging
stem: Application Insights shows the ingestion worker as a separate operation from the API that triggers it. What restores one end-to-end trace?

options.text: Propagate `traceparent` through the queue message
Increase sampling so more of the worker's telemetry is retained
Point both components at the same Application Insights resource
Add a custom property holding the product id to both sides

explanation: Correlation travels in the message, not in the connection string. Without the trace context crossing the queue hop, the worker starts a brand-new operation id and the two halves can never be joined.

whyWrong.B: Sampling changes how much is kept, not whether the two operations are related.
whyWrong.C: A shared resource is necessary but not sufficient — they would still be two unrelated operations.
whyWrong.D: A shared custom property lets you search manually; it does not build a trace.

stem: Put the rebuild in the order that fixes Fabrikam's problems without changing the Cosmos DB account or partition key.

options.text: Switch the change feed to all-versions-and-deletes mode so deletions are visible
Restructure the nightly job as a durable fan-out of short activities
Send the work through bulk execution with retry-after handling
Propagate trace context from the API into the worker

explanation: Fix the thing that stops the run finishing first — a job that never completes makes everything downstream unmeasurable. Then smooth the writes so it completes reliably, then correct the stale index, and finally restore correlation so the next problem is diagnosable. Ordering questions on the exam usually reward this shape: restore completion, then correctness, then observability.

docs.title: Change feed in Azure Cosmos DB

hint: Something has to run to completion before anything else can be judged. Leave the diagnostics until the pipeline works.
